newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bank Austria sees extra cash from CA deal.
newsitem.headline: Bank Austria sees extra cash from CA deal.

text.p: Bank Austria said on Sunday its takeover of Austrian establishment bank Creditanstalt would make the country's coveted banking sector fit for Europe while putting wads of extra cash into shareholders' pockets.
"Based on conservative estimates the future results of the Bank Austria-CA group should bring in extra earnings potential of several billion schillings," the bank said in a statement.

Bank Austria's visibly contented chief executive Gerhard Randa told a news conference called only hours after the politically charged deal was closed that the merger should result in a doubling of earnings per share over five years.

"We are assuming that in the next five years earnings per share double (from 1995's 43 schillings per share)," he said, brandishing the signed contract for the state's 70 percent voting stake in the former banker to Austro-Hungarian emperors.
Randa later admitted the merger of Austria's two top banks would result in "substantial" charges against earnings, but added that current-year profits should still see an increase.
"The charges against earnings will be substantial -- and still our earnings will be better in 1997," he told Reuters.

The 52-year old dapper chief executive, who overnight became the single most powerful figure in Austria's business life, said the bank's 1996 parent operating profit was expected to reach 5.1 billion schillings, while net earnings should be "a trace below" the 2.2 billion schillings reported for 1995.

Bank Austria, supported by the ruling Social Democrats, won the seven-year battle for Creditanstalt against a rival bid from a consortium led by insurer EA-Generali, backed by the conservative coalition partner, the People's Party.

Randa said his bank would be able to finance the 17.2 billion schillings it offered for control of its main rival from own resources. Still, he said Bank Austria was likely to tap capital markets this year to top up its reserves.
"I would assume that there will be a capital increase before the end of the year," he said without giving details.

The marriage of Austria's two top banks will create a financial powerhouse with some 1,300 billion schillings, employing more than 16,000 people -- a giant by Austrian standards that would be part of Europe's top 30 banks.
They will have a domestic market share of 25 percent in asset terms, and control 70 percent of commercial banking, 80 percent of Vienna bourse trade and half of export financing.

"It's a real historic step for us, the biggest step we ever took," Randa said. "It's good that we got this chance on the eve of Europe's planned single currency. We will see foreign banks invading our business and we need to be a strong bank."
Randa added a planned restructuring of the merged banks would make them more competitive not just in Europe but worldwide and help to strengthen project and export financing.

The Social Democrat-ruled City of Vienna effectively holds 46 percent of Bank Austria's voting shares through its foundation Anteilsverwaltung Zentralsparkasse (AVZ). Vienna guarantees the bank's liabilities, ensuring an AAA rating.
The Republic of Austria controls 19 percent of equity.
According to the coalition agreement the state's stake will be floated immediately, while the influence of the City of Vienna's AVZ foundation will be cut to below 20 percent within seven years.
Randa said the fact that AVZ would continue to guarantee Bank Austria's liabilities would most likely ensure a confirmation of its AAA long-term rating.
